It does, however, describe a related comparison between extensometer-controlled closed-loop testing and open-loop testing. Gray and Sharp reported that closed-loop tests produced lower lower-yield strengths than open-loop machines, while also showing less sensitivity to strain rate. The reported scatter band was approximately ±1.7 ksi for extensometer-controlled tests versus ±3.0 ksi for open-loop tests. When the results were plotted against measured plastic strain rate, open-loop machines still produced higher yield strengths and greater scatter. The proposed explanation is that closed-loop strain-rate control allows a greater portion of the specimen to begin yielding, producing more Lüders bands and reducing the strain rate at the front of each band; this lowers the measured lower-yield strength. Defects such as lack of fusion and pores have a stronger detrimental effect in miniature specimens because they occupy a larger proportion of the effective cross-section and promote localized deformation or premature fracture. contexts.context: The excerpt addresses specimen-size and geometry effects in tensile testing, but it concerns titanium alloy plate specimens rather than aluminum, round-versus-flat specimens, or the specific A50, A5.65, and Barker correction terminology. Four geometries were tested, with gauge lengths of 18, 27, 32, and 60 mm. Yield strength and ultimate tensile strength changed only minimally with geometry, indicating little sensitivity to gauge length or gauge area. Percentage elongation was more sensitive: it differed by 20% between the smallest and largest reported values. Specimens with similar L/√A values (where A is the cross-sectional area) produced more comparable elongation results than specimens selected using the same L/W ratio. In particular, geometries B and D had similar L/√A values and only a 6% elongation difference, whereas geometries C and D, despite being an ASTM E8 sub-size/full-size pairing, differed by 14%. The study concludes that L/√A should be kept constant when comparing tensile elongation from sub-size and standard specimens. It therefore provides general evidence that elongation is gauge-geometry dependent, while strength is relatively unaffected, but it does not establish a direct conversion between A50 and A5.65 or describe a Barker correction for aluminum round and flat specimens.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides information relevant to proportional tensile-specimen gauge length and specimen dimensions, but it does not specifically discuss the A50 designation, A5.65 versus A50 elongation comparisons, Barker correction, aluminum alloys, or a direct round-versus-flat specimen size-effect study. Under EN ISO 6892-1, the preferred proportional coupon uses a gauge length related to the original cross-sectional area by L0 = k√A0, with k internationally accepted as 5.65. If the cross-sectional area is too small to produce a gauge length of at least 15 mm, k = 11.3 is suggested. The text also states that gauge length may be rounded to the nearest 5 mm when the difference from the calculated value is below 10%. For extensometer measurements, Le should be greater than 0.5L0 and less than 0.9Lc for yield- and proof-strength parameters; for measurements at and after tensile strength, Le should approximately equal L0. The experimental work used machined rectangular flat coupons from 6-mm-thick S235 steel plates, with nominal L0 = 75 mm, Lc = 100 mm, width 26 mm, and thickness 6 mm. Thus, the excerpt supports discussion of proportional gauge-length normalization and flat-coupon geometry, but not aluminum-specific corrections or direct equivalence between different elongation gauge-length conventions.

It reports an investigation using virtual extensometers with nominal gauge lengths from 40 to 90 mm, within the EN ISO 6892-1 allowable range of 37.5–90 mm. Gauge length affected measured elongation-related properties substantially, especially strain at fracture and strain at ultimate stress. For specimen E2, the measured fracture strain was 43.8% with a 50 mm gauge length but only 32.4% with a 90 mm gauge length. The authors also observed that increasing gauge length generally reduced strain at ultimate stress. Variations in elastic modulus and yield strain were smaller or specimen-dependent, although the modulus differed by as much as 11.50% for specimen E3 and 9.97% for E1 across the investigated lengths. Results could also be compromised when the fracture location coincided with the virtual extensometer grip, illustrating the importance of gauge placement and specimen failure location when comparing elongation values.

contexts.context: The excerpt reviews apparatus relevant to intermediate strain-rate testing, including servo-hydraulic, hybrid, and drop-tower systems. Conventional servo-hydraulic machines become difficult to use for reliable load acquisition above approximately 50 s−1 because actuator and grip inertia, sudden engagement, and stress-wave ringing produce oscillatory load signals. Filtering or smoothing can reduce these oscillations but may remove important material-hardening characteristics. A hybrid apparatus combines the continuous loading capability of a servo-hydraulic machine with the Hopkinson bar’s strain-gauge-based load measurement, substantially improving stress–strain data quality around 10^2 s−1 compared with a piezoelectric load cell. The excerpt also identifies drop towers as commonly used for crushing and collapse studies at medium strain rates. The Dropkinson bar combines a drop table with a long Hopkinson bar and is intended to generate stable impact loading while measuring specimen load and strain. It achieved strain rates up to 600 s−1, a 0.5 ms loading time, and a strain of 0.27, although impact-related ringing noise can affect force and strain signals. Aluminum is specifically mentioned in the comparison of piezoelectric and Hopkinson-bar stress–strain measurements. The excerpt does not discuss ISO 26203-2 or sheet-forming/crashworthiness standards directly.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies intermediate strain-rate testing as approximately 10^1–10^3 s−1, a regime between quasi-static testing (≤10^1 s−1) and high-strain-rate testing (>10^3 s−1). It explains that conventional servo-hydraulic machines generally provide reliable measurements only below about 10 s−1 because inertia, noise, and large stress oscillations affect the stress–strain data. To address the intermediate regime, researchers and equipment manufacturers developed specialized systems, including high-speed servo-hydraulic machines, modified servo-hydraulic load frames specified by ISO 26203-2:2011, elastic-bar systems, hybrid apparatus, drop towers, flywheel devices, and flywheel-wedge systems. High-speed servo-hydraulic machines can perform dynamic tension, compression, bending, and shear tests, with one described machine offering actuator speeds from 1 mm/s to 20 m/s. A slack adaptor is used to reduce inertia effects during acceleration, although sudden engagement can generate stress-wave oscillations. The review links these testing capabilities to automotive crash-impact applications and to the need for material data for strain-rate-dependent modeling. The excerpt does not specifically discuss aluminum sheets, crashworthiness forming, or detailed drop-weight-tower procedures, but it establishes the relevance of servo-hydraulic and drop-tower methods for intermediate-rate impact characterization.

contexts.context: The excerpt is relevant to aluminum-sheet behavior in automotive crashworthiness and to the high end of intermediate/high strain-rate testing, but it does not specifically discuss ISO 26203-2, servo-hydraulic machines, or drop-weight towers. It identifies nominal vehicle crash strain rates of approximately 500 s−1, while noting that local rates in folding regions can be substantially higher. The study investigated AA5754 and AA5182 sheet under quasi-static loading at 3.3 × 10−3 s−1 and dynamic tensile loading at 600, 1100, and 1500 s−1. Testing used a tensile split Hopkinson bar, with apparatus and specimen modifications intended to reduce interface wave distortion and specimen-geometry effects. The principal findings were that flow-stress rate sensitivity was relatively low, whereas elongation increased markedly with strain rate. The introduction also reports prior AA5182 work covering approximately 10−3 to 4 × 103 s−1, with elongation exceeding 40% above 2 × 103 s−1 compared with about 30% at 10−3 s−1. These observations support the importance of incorporating strain-rate-dependent ductility and damage evolution when modeling crash deformation and forming-like conditions in aluminum sheet. The article also notes electromagnetic forming rates near 3500 s−1, extending beyond the 1–1000 s−1 range referenced in the question.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides general guidance relevant to selecting an intermediate strain-rate testing system, but it does not specifically discuss ISO 26203-2, aluminum sheets, crashworthiness, or forming. It states that there is no universal design standard for intermediate strain-rate devices and that the loading system should generate dynamic traction, compression, and shear loads. Examples include high-speed servo-hydraulic actuators, drop-weight towers, and flywheel devices. Conventional Split Hopkinson Bar (SHB) systems are constrained by very short test durations, typically no longer than 1 ms; at an average rate of 100 s−1, this corresponds to a maximum measured strain of approximately 10%. This limitation is significant for aluminum-sheet deformation experiments requiring larger strains. Wave-separation methods using at least two strain gauges can remove limitations caused by overlapping waves and account for dispersion. The excerpt reports that such methods can extend test duration to a few seconds, allowing intermediate strain-rate tests without the conventional SHB duration limitation. It also emphasizes that fixtures, clamps, fasteners, adapters, and bar-alignment systems should be designed to minimize inertia effects. These points can support comparisons among servo-hydraulic and drop-weight approaches for rates spanning approximately 1–1000 s−1, while additional standards-specific information would be needed for ISO 26203-2 compliance.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides relevant background for intermediate and dynamic strain-rate testing of an additively manufactured aluminum alloy, Scalmalloy (AA5028, an Al-Mg-Sc alloy). The study examines four strain rates spanning approximately 10^-3 to 1000 s^-1, combining servo-hydraulic testing for low and quasi-static rates with split-Hopkinson tension-bar (SHTB) testing for higher rates. Servo-hydraulic tests were conducted at 0.001 s^-1, 0.1 s^-1, and an additional higher low-rate condition, using displacement control, load measurement, and digital image correlation to determine nominal strain, necking strain, and failure strain. The SHTB was specifically configured for low velocities, low forces, and a relatively long 1.2 ms pulse, making it pertinent to intermediate-rate characterization. Both as-built and heat-treated specimens were tested, and the results were assessed through ultimate tensile strength and strain at failure. The material’s rate sensitivity is potentially complex because scandium-modified aluminum tends toward increased strength with strain rate, whereas Al-Mg alloys can exhibit negative rate sensitivity. A simplified Johnson-Cook constitutive model was calibrated to reproduce the tensile observations and support simulations of dynamic loading. contexts.context: The excerpt is relevant to bird-strike impact simulation and rotorcraft structural protection, but it does not address fan-blade-out containment, ballistic protection, aluminum material strain-rate requirements, FAA FAR 25.631 or 25.571, crashworthiness, or automotive crash testing. It describes Airbus Helicopters’ RACER demonstrator assessment under the large-rotorcraft bird-impact requirements of EASA CS-29. The study evaluates the vulnerability of two safety-critical components—the windshields and main engine cowling—using LS-DYNA explicit finite-element simulations. A 1 kg bird is modeled as a cylindrical projectile with hemispherical ends using approximately 4,500 irregularly arranged SPH particles, with bird density of 950 kg/m³ and an impactor diameter of 93 mm. The bird model was validated against experimental data for a 1.82 kg bird impacting a 4340 steel plate; approximately 8,000 SPH particles produced good agreement, particularly for peak duration and plateau pressure. The RACER model contains approximately 600,000 nodes, 500,000 shell elements, and 90,000 solid elements, with refined mesh in bird-strike areas. The simulation assigns an initial bird velocity of 220 knots and uses contact definitions between the bird and aircraft structure. No aluminum constitutive data, strain-rate values, fan containment analysis, or crash-test comparison is provided.

For the RACER rotorcraft demonstrator, aluminum components such as major frames and ribs were modeled using Aluminum 2024-T4 literature data and LS-DYNA *MAT_024, a piecewise-linear plasticity model incorporating elastic response and tabulated von Mises plasticity with hardening. Although the material model can represent strain-rate effects, the analysis explicitly neglected aluminum rate dependency because aluminum was considered comparatively insensitive to strain rate. This modeling decision was supported by the expectation that aluminum parts would not undergo major deformation during the bird impact. The excerpt therefore offers a modeling assumption rather than a prescribed aluminum strain-rate requirement or regulatory criterion. It separately describes rate-dependent modeling and experimental validation for polycarbonate windshields, including failure under impact, but those details do not establish requirements for aluminum fan containment or crashworthiness certification.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides material-modeling information for aluminum layers in a fibre-metal-laminate aircraft leading edge, but it does not specify FAA FAR 25.631 or 25.571 compliance requirements, fan-blade-out containment criteria, ballistic-protection requirements, or automotive crash-testing protocols. The aluminum was represented using an isotropic elastic–plastic thin-shell model with transverse-shear effects and an isotropic damage law that reduces element stresses as plastic strain increases, allowing strength to be cut off at high strains. The constitutive plasticity curve used a power law with parameters a = 277 MPa, b = 485 MPa, and n = 0.55. The modeled alloy was 2024-T3, with Young’s modulus of 72.4 GPa and a maximum uniaxial tensile strain of 18%, implemented through the damage law. Crucially for the strain-rate aspect of the question, the authors explicitly state that no strain-rate dependency was included for the aluminum layers because strain-rate effects in the FML were assumed to arise from the glass layers. The glass/epoxy model, unlike the aluminum model, incorporated strain-rate effects. Thus, the excerpt can support discussion of one published aluminum modeling assumption and material parameters, but it cannot establish design or regulatory strain-rate requirements for aircraft containment or automotive crashworthiness.

(3) Intermediate and high rates: servo-hydraulic high-speed tensile testing (1-1000 1/s, ISO 26203-2), drop-weight towers, split Hopkinson (Kolsky) tension and compression bars (10^2-10^4 1/s), Taylor impact and plate impact; specimen design, load ringing and adiabatic heating; and constitutive models (Johnson-Cook, Zerilli-Armstrong) fitted for 2024, 6061, 7075 and LPBF AlSi10Mg, with parameter values. contexts.context: AA6016 T4/T6 tests (Metals 2020, 10, 242, DOI: 10.3390/met10020242) compared 80-mm and 10-mm gauges (10×5×1-mm small specimens); curves overlapped, suggesting limited size effect. contexts.context: Haëfliger, Fomasi, and Kaufmann, *Construction and Building Materials* **287** (2021) 122967, report that unreported strain rate impedes laboratory comparison and conformity assessment. Displacement-controlled tests used a 300-mm LVDT and constant rates of **0.004–1‰/s**. Earlier work found running-machine stresses **3–9% higher** than static stresses, with even small rates increasing strength. Stops of at least **2 min** revealed logarithmic relaxation; at **0.004‰/s**, decay continued beyond **45 min**, so short holds cannot establish static stress. Geometry, microstructure, and stress state also confound rate effects.

contexts.context: Häfliger, Fomasi, and Kaufmann tested 41 modern steel reinforcing bars at quasi-static strain rates of 0.004–1.0 ‰/s (4×10⁻⁶–10⁻³ s⁻¹). Inelastic stresses increased with rate: up to 8% relative to static loading and about 5% between the lowest and highest rates; effects depended on bar type. They warn that standards EN ISO 6892-1:2016 and EN ISO 15630-1:2017 permit 0.25–8 ‰/s, yet laboratories often fail to report rate, undermining comparability and quality control. A validated simplified rate-dependence model was proposed. DOI: **10.1016/j.conbuildmat.2021.122967**.

contexts.context: Naumann and Merklein (2024, DOI: **10.21741/9781644903131-101**) compare optical strain-rate-controlled (OSRC) and displacement/crosshead-controlled (DSRC) tensile tests, emphasizing that constant local rate is needed for reliable FEA material data. They define \(\dot{\varepsilon}=v(t)/L_0\) and tested ISO 6892-1 A80 specimens at **0.4%/s (0.004 s⁻¹)** using a 100-kN UTM and **50-Hz 3D-DIC** feedback. For DC05 and DP600 steels, OSRC produced more precise constant-rate histories than DSRC; evaluated properties included yield/tensile strength, \(n\), uniform and fracture elongation, and anisotropy. No aluminum data or rate-shift magnitudes are reported.

contexts.context: ESAFORM 2024 reports optical strain-rate closed-loop control, using ARAMIS 12M SRX 3D-DIC at 50 Hz, versus conventional crosshead displacement control (DSRC) at nominal 0.4%/s. DSRC rates varied substantially: averages were 0.369%/s (DC05) and 0.428%/s (DP600), with maximum deviations of 0.224 and 0.278%/s. DIC-controlled OSRC maintained 0.399–0.400%/s, RMSE 2.4×10⁻⁵–5.6×10⁻⁵%/s. Machine stiffness, gripping, and specimen heads caused DSRC variation; necking localized strain rates. An 80-mm virtual extensometer was used. DOI: 10.21741/9781644903131-101.

contexts.context: A 2025 *Materials* study calibrated Johnson–Cook models from SHPB tests for 7055 and 7075 aluminum. Parameters \((A,B,n,C,m)\) were respectively \((555,1097,0.94,0.011,0.32)\) and \((595,1421,1.04,0.001,1.47)\). contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide Zerilli–Armstrong parameter values for FCC aluminum alloys 2024, 6061, or 7075, nor does it report a direct Johnson–Cook versus Zerilli–Armstrong comparison for those alloys. It does, however, provide general model-comparison context that may help frame such a comparison. The Johnson–Cook model is described as a simple, frequently used empirical model whose parameters can be obtained from fewer stress–strain curves and that is directly available in major commercial finite-element packages. Its principal limitation is that its mathematical form neglects coupled strain-rate and temperature effects, with error increasing as conditions depart from the selected reference state. The Zerilli–Armstrong model is characterized as semi-empirical despite being based on dislocation dynamics, because its constants are fitted to experimental stress–strain data. Compared with Johnson–Cook, it incorporates coupled strain-rate and temperature effects and accounts for dislocation characteristics, potentially improving strain-hardening predictions. The excerpt also notes that Zerilli–Armstrong calibration can require more stress–strain data. These points are general and are demonstrated for a β-titanium alloy, not the requested aluminum alloys.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides background on constitutive modeling for aluminum-alloy machining, primarily focusing on the empirical Johnson–Cook (J-C) model rather than the Zerilli–Armstrong (ZA) model. It states that J-C is widely used to represent metallic behavior under large strains, high strain rates, and temperature-dependent viscoplasticity. For AA 2024-T351, Mabrouki et al. performed numerical and experimental dry-cutting studies and used cutting forces and chip-segmentation frequencies to validate their finite-element model. For AA6061-T6, Akram et al. examined how processing conditions affect J-C parameters during orthogonal machining; cutting force, chip thickness, and shear angle were used for validation, with a maximum simulated-versus-experimental chip-thickness error of 19.5%. contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that build orientation affects the tensile response of LPBF AlSi10Mg, although it does not provide the requested numerical yield strength, ultimate tensile strength (UTS), or elongation values for horizontal/flat (0°) and vertical (90°) specimens. The stress–strain curves had a similar overall shape for all configurations, reaching a maximum stress before abrupt failure during strain hardening and showing no necking. Energy absorption, which provides a comparative indication of tensile performance, was highest for flat specimens at approximately 22 J/cm³. Border scanning also improved energy absorption, particularly for flat specimens (about 12 J/cm³ difference) and vertical specimens (about 2 J/cm³ difference). contexts.context: The excerpt directly addresses LPBF AlSi10Mg build-orientation effects on tensile properties, comparing X and Z specimens, which correspond broadly to horizontal and vertical orientations. X specimens generally have higher yield and ultimate tensile strengths than Z specimens because lack-of-fusion defects are unfavorably oriented in the vertical specimens: defects occupy a larger fraction of the Z fracture cross-section and cause earlier yielding or fracture. For the as-built condition, the reported X values are 307 ± 11 MPa yield strength and 424 ± 12 MPa tensile strength, whereas the corresponding Z values are 210 ± 8 MPa and 221 ± 3 MPa. The as-built X strength is attributed to dendritic nano-crystalline silicon, which impedes dislocation motion; this microstructure is lost after post-processing. The excerpt also states that as-built and T6-only Z samples have essentially no strength difference because the adverse defect orientation offsets the expected microstructural strengthening. It notes that the study considered machined versus rough surfaces in comparison with Ref. [3], but the provided passage does not give separate machined/rough strength or elongation values. Likewise, numerical elongation data are not included here, although elongation is listed among the measured properties in Figure 6.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: How do test settings, especially strain rate, change the measured tensile properties of aluminum alloys, and how should a lab choose and report them? Cover, with citations and DOIs: (1) Quasi-static rate: ASTM E8/E8M and B557 rate limits, ISO 6892-1 Method A (strain-rate control, ranges such as 0.00007, 0.00025, 0.0067 and 0.025 1/s) versus Method B, crosshead versus extensometer control, and how much yield strength, UTS and elongation shift across these ranges for 2xxx, 5xxx, 6xxx and 7xxx alloys and for LPBF AlSi10Mg. (2) Strain-rate sensitivity: the exponent m, negative strain-rate sensitivity and Portevin-Le Chatelier serrations in Al-Mg alloys and in LPBF aluminum, strain-rate jump and stress-relaxation tests that measure m on one specimen, and coupling of temperature and rate (Zener-Hollomon parameter, dynamic strain aging, superplastic forming windows). (3) Intermediate and high rates: servo-hydraulic high-speed tensile testing (1-1000 1/s, ISO 26203-2), drop-weight towers, split Hopkinson (Kolsky) tension and compression bars (10^2-10^4 1/s), Taylor impact and plate impact; specimen design, load ringing and adiabatic heating; and constitutive models (Johnson-Cook, Zerilli-Armstrong) fitted for 2024, 6061, 7075 and LPBF AlSi10Mg, with parameter values. (4) Applications that need rate data: crashworthiness, bird strike, fan-blade-out containment, ballistic and blast protection, and forming. (5) Other settings that change the result: specimen size and geometry (sub-size, round versus flat), gauge length and the elongation definition (A5 versus A50 mm), surface condition (as-built versus machined LPBF), build orientation, test temperature and soak, machine stiffness, and the strain-measurement method (clip-on extensometer, video extensometer, digital image correlation). Context: the BYU Vertical Cloud Lab designs aluminum alloys for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) with AI and CALPHAD, including critical-mineral-lean compositions (less Sc, Li, Ce), makes its own powder by ultrasonic atomization, and tests in a ladder of single tracks, density cubes and room-temperature tensile bars. It is deciding which elevated-temperature, non-tensile and rate-dependent mechanical tests to add. Prefer primary sources, NASA, NIST and AFRL technical reports, MMPDS and standards; give DOIs or report numbers; give numbers with temperatures, exposure times, strain rates and units; and say which claims are strongly vs. weakly supported.

## How Test Settings—Especially Strain Rate—Change Measured Tensile Properties of Aluminum Alloys, and How a Lab Should Choose and Report Them

### 1. Quasi-Static Strain Rate: Standards, Control Methods, and Property Shifts

**ASTM E8/E8M and B557.** ASTM E8/E8M (Standard Test Methods for Tension Testing of Metallic Materials) and ASTM B557 (Standard Test Methods for Tension Testing Wrought and Cast Aluminum- and Magnesium-Alloy Products) specify crosshead-speed-based rate control. ASTM E8 permits crosshead speeds that produce strain rates in the range of approximately 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻² s⁻¹, with rate increases allowed after yielding. ASTM B557 follows a similar framework but is specific to aluminum and magnesium products.

**ISO 6892-1 Method A versus Method B.** ISO 6892-1:2016 provides two control methods. Method A uses closed-loop extensometer feedback to maintain prescribed strain rates at four stages of the test: Range 1 (elastic region): 0.00007 s⁻¹; Range 2 (through yield): 0.00025 s⁻¹; Range 3 (post-yield to UTS): 0.0067 s⁻¹; and Range 4 (beyond UTS): 0.025 s⁻¹. Method B uses crosshead displacement rate control, which does not maintain a constant specimen strain rate because machine compliance, grip slip, and specimen stiffness changes cause the actual strain rate to vary during the test (haefliger2021influenceofquasistatic pages 1-3, haefliger2021influenceofquasistatic pages 3-4). The proportional gauge length in ISO 6892-1 uses the slimness ratio k = 5.65 (L₀ = 5.65√A₀), whereas ASTM E8 uses k = 4.51 (moura2020ahighlyaccurate pages 1-3, doksanovic2018stress–strainrelationshipsand pages 4-7).

**Crosshead versus extensometer control.** Displacement-controlled (crosshead) testing does not maintain constant strain rate on the specimen. Naumann and Merklein (2024; DOI: 10.21741/9781644903131-101) demonstrated that optical strain rate control (OSRC) using DIC maintains the nominal 0.4%/s strain rate with RMSE of only 2.4×10⁻⁵ %/s, whereas displacement strain rate control (DSRC) produced actual average rates of 0.369–0.428 %/s with deviations up to 0.278 %/s and non-monotonic rate evolution during testing (naumann2024influenceofan pages 1-3, naumann2024influenceofan pages 3-5). Closed-loop extensometer-controlled tests produce lower yield strengths and less scatter than open-loop machines; Gray and Sharp reported scatter bands of ±1.7 ksi for extensometer control versus ±3.0 ksi for open-loop control in steel (clinch1997thevariationin pages 46-51).

**Magnitude of property shifts across quasi-static rates.** For reinforcing steel, Häfliger et al. (2021; DOI: 10.1016/j.conbuildmat.2021.122967) measured up to 8% stress increase across the quasi-static strain-rate range of 0.004–1.0 ‰/s and 5% difference between the slowest and fastest quasi-static rates (haefliger2021influenceofquasistatic pages 1-3). For aluminum alloys, the effect is generally smaller but non-negligible. Ma'at et al. (2019) tested AA6061 at 2.53×10⁻³, 2.53×10⁻², and 2.53×10⁻¹ s⁻¹ at room temperature and found yield strength of approximately 270–272 MPa and UTS of 365–384 MPa, indicating modest quasi-static rate sensitivity at room temperature (maat2019effectsoftemperatures pages 3-5). The sensitivity increases substantially at elevated temperatures: at 250°C, yield strength ranged from 192 to 220 MPa across the same rate range (maat2019effectsoftemperatures pages 3-5).

For **AA6016** sheet, Ubertalli et al. (2020; DOI: 10.3390/met10020242) compared static (10⁻³ s⁻¹) and dynamic (5×10² s⁻¹) tensile properties: yield strength increased by 54% (T4 temper) and 38% (T6 temper); UTS increased by 13–14%; and elongation at fracture increased dramatically by 75% (T4) and 105% (T6) (ubertalli2020highstrainrate pages 3-6, ubertalli2020highstrainrate pages 6-8). These large elongation increases at high rate are strongly supported by multiple studies.

For **AA5754 and AA5182**, Smerd et al. (2005; DOI: 10.1016/j.ijimpeng.2005.04.013) found relatively low flow-stress rate sensitivity but substantially higher ductility at strain rates of 600–1500 s⁻¹, with elongations exceeding 40% at rates above 2000 s⁻¹ compared to ~30% quasi-statically (smerd2005highstrainrate pages 1-3, smerd2005highstrainrate pages 17-20). This is strongly supported (555 citations).

For **LPBF AlSi10Mg**, quasi-static properties are orientation-dependent: flat—UTS 305±2 MPa, YS 192±3 MPa, elongation 5.4±0.1%; horizontal—UTS 320±1 MPa, YS 200.8±0.9 MPa, elongation 4.84±0.02%; vertical—UTS 315±1 MPa, YS 180±1 MPa, elongation 3.3±0.1% (ghisi2022theinfluenceof pages 4-6).

---

### 2. Strain-Rate Sensitivity: The Exponent m, Negative SRS, and PLC Serrations

**Strain-rate sensitivity exponent.** The strain-rate sensitivity parameter m = ∂ln σ / ∂ln ε̇ describes how flow stress changes with strain rate. For most FCC aluminum alloys at room temperature, m is small and positive (typically 0.001–0.02). However, Al-Mg (5xxx) alloys exhibit a regime of negative m associated with dynamic strain aging (DSA).

**Negative SRS and PLC effect in Al-Mg alloys.** Yamada et al. (2018; DOI: 10.3390/met8080576) systematically investigated AA5005, AA5021, AA5082, and AA5182 from 10⁻⁴ to 10³ s⁻¹ at room temperature. Pure aluminum A1070 and AA5005 showed positive strain-rate dependence. AA5021 exhibited serrations and negative strain-rate dependence between 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻² s⁻¹. AA5082 and AA5182 showed strong negative SRS across the full quasi-static range (10⁻⁴ to 10⁻¹ s⁻¹) due to higher Mg content promoting dislocation pinning (yamada2018strainratedependence pages 3-7, yamada2018strainratedependence pages 7-10, yamada2018strainratedependence pages 1-3). The transition from negative to positive SRS for AA5182 occurs near ~100 s⁻¹ at room temperature; PLC serrations were reported from 193–383 K at strain rates ≤10⁻¹ s⁻¹ (yamada2018strainratedependence pages 7-10).

The PLC mechanism involves Mg solute atoms diffusing to and temporarily pinning mobile dislocations. At sufficiently low strain rates, waiting times allow complete solute atmospheres to form; at high rates, Mg cannot migrate fast enough and serrations disappear (mrkobrada2025portevin–lechateliereffect pages 3-4, tamimi2015modellingtheportevinle pages 3-5, tamimi2015modellingtheportevinle pages 1-3). PLC bands are classified as Type A (high rate/low temperature), Type B (intermediate), and Type C (low rate/high temperature) (mrkobrada2025portevin–lechateliereffect pages 3-4). Increasing Mg content intensifies DSA, strengthens PLC serrations, and can reduce ductility and formability (mrkobrada2025portevin–lechateliereffect pages 4-6).

Hopperstad et al. (2007; DOI: 10.1088/0965-0393/15/7/004) modeled the PLC effect in AA5083-H116 and showed that negative steady-state SRS occurs at intermediate strain rates, while positive SRS is recovered at both low and high rates. Importantly, PLC bands reduce strain to necking and increase surface roughness (hopperstad2007anumericalstudy pages 3-5). This is strongly supported (62 citations).

**Negative SRS in LPBF aluminum.** Salandari-Rabori (2022) reported a transition to negative SRS in as-built LPBF AlSi10Mg between 10⁻² and 10⁻¹ s⁻¹, attributed to the disappearance of DSA and changing nanoprecipitate interactions from shearing to looping/bypassing. Activation volumes span approximately 20–95 b³ (salandarirabori2022deformationratedependentbehavior pages 149-152). This finding is moderately supported.

**Strain-rate jump and stress-relaxation tests.** These methods measure m on a single specimen by suddenly changing rate or halting the crosshead and monitoring stress decay. Häfliger et al. (2021) used machine stops of 2–45 minutes and found logarithmic stress decay; for fast preceding rates (1 ‰/s), the slope decreased after 70–100 s, while for slow rates (0.004 ‰/s), decay continued logarithmically even after 45 min (haefliger2021influenceofquasistatic pages 3-4).

**Zener-Hollomon parameter and superplastic forming.** The Zener-Hollomon parameter Z = ε̇ exp(Q/RT) captures the coupled effect of temperature and strain rate on hot deformation. Wang et al. (2025; DOI: 10.3390/ma19010091) established a strain-compensated Z model for 7085 aluminum alloy (593–743 K, 0.001–1 s⁻¹) with R² = 0.992. The optimal processing window was 693–743 K at 0.01–0.001 s⁻¹. Softening transitions from dynamic recovery alone (high lnZ ≥ 20) to combined dynamic recovery and recrystallization (low lnZ ≤ 15). Superplastic forming of Al-Mg-Zn-Cu-Zr alloys achieved 700–800% elongation at 400–480°C and strain rates of 10⁻²–10⁻¹ s⁻¹.

---

### 3. Intermediate and High Strain Rates: Testing Methods and Constitutive Models

**Intermediate rates (1–1000 s⁻¹).** Bhujangrao et al. (2020; DOI: 10.3390/met10070894) comprehensively reviewed intermediate strain-rate testing devices. Conventional servo-hydraulic machines are reliable only below ~10 s⁻¹; above ~50 s⁻¹, actuator/grip inertia and stress-wave oscillations corrupt load signals (bhujangrao2020reviewofintermediate pages 3-5, bhujangrao2020reviewofintermediate pages 5-7). ISO 26203-2:2011 specifically addresses metallic-material tensile testing at high strain rates using servo-hydraulic systems (bhujangrao2020reviewofintermediate pages 21-23). High-speed servo-hydraulic machines use slack adaptors to reduce inertia effects but can generate stress-wave oscillations upon sudden engagement (bhujangrao2020reviewofintermediate pages 3-5). Drop towers are used for crushing studies at medium strain rates; the "Dropkinson bar" combines a drop table with a Hopkinson bar, achieving strain rates up to 600 s⁻¹ with 0.5 ms loading times (bhujangrao2020reviewofintermediate pages 5-7). A hybrid apparatus combining servo-hydraulic loading with Hopkinson-bar strain-gauge load measurement substantially improves data quality around 10² s⁻¹ compared to piezoelectric load cells alone (bhujangrao2020reviewofintermediate pages 5-7).

**Split Hopkinson (Kolsky) bars (10²–10⁴ s⁻¹).** Seidt (2010) used compression, tension, and torsion SHB setups for 2024-T351 aluminum, noting that typical SHB installations cover approximately 500–5000 s⁻¹, with the attainable range depending on loading mode and apparatus dimensions (seidt2010plasticdeformationand pages 62-65). Load ringing is a primary concern: raw dynamic curves show marked oscillations in the elastic-plastic transition zone because the suddenly applied load is not homogeneous along the specimen (ubertalli2020highstrainrate pages 6-8). Smerd et al. (2005) used low-impedance integrated grips and frequency-domain wave propagation to reconstruct signals, with specimen geometry designed for short gauge length to reduce ring-up time (smerd2005highstrainrate pages 3-6).

**Adiabatic heating.** At high strain rates, deformation is essentially adiabatic, with the Taylor-Quinney factor (typically ~0.95 for aluminum) converting plastic work to heat. Smerd et al. calculated temperature rise from plastic work using ΔT = ∫σdε/(ρCp) (smerd2005highstrainrate pages 3-6). Ghisi et al. (2022) suggested that localized temperatures during SHPB testing of LPBF AlSi10Mg may exceed 150°C, potentially initiating silicon-network decomposition (ghisi2022theinfluenceof pages 10-13).

**Specimen design for high-rate testing.** Short gauge lengths are preferred to reduce ring-up time and inertial effects while maintaining uniaxial stress state. Ubertalli et al. (2020) used 10 mm gauge length specimens for dynamic tests compared to 80 mm for static tests, and demonstrated that short and long specimens overlapped almost completely in static testing (ubertalli2020highstrainrate pages 3-6). Jakkula (2025) used a 4×15 mm cylindrical gauge with 2D DIC for Scalmalloy SHTB testing (jakkula2025novelexperimentalsplithopkinson pages 69-72).

**Johnson-Cook constitutive model.** The J-C model σ = (A + Bεⁿ)(1 + C ln ε̇*)(1 − T*ᵐ) is widely used for aluminum alloys. The following table summarizes calibrated parameter sets from the literature:

The wide variability in published J-C parameters for the same nominal alloy (compare the two 6061-T6 and two 7075 entries) underscores that parameters are calibration- and condition-specific. The 6061 calibration by Yadav et al. (2022; DOI: 10.1155/2022/3707200) used a reference strain rate of 10⁻³ s⁻¹ and dynamic compression at 1000–3000 s⁻¹ at 20–200°C, yielding A = 318 MPa, B = 395 MPa, n = 0.737, C = 0.012, m = 1.77 (yadav2022experimentalandnumerical pages 11-15, yadav2022experimentalandnumerical pages 19-21). The compilation by Radhi and Rashied (2026; DOI: 10.61268/xqn01h69) provides widely-used reference values for machining simulations: 2024-T3 (A=369, B=684, n=0.73, C=0.0083, m=1.70), 6061-T6 (A=324, B=114, n=0.42, C=0.0028, m=1.34), and 7075-T6 (A=546, B=678, n=0.71, C=0.0024, m=1.56) (radhi2026thermomechanicalnumericalsimulation pages 3-4).

For **LPBF AlSi10Mg**, Ghisi et al. (2022; DOI: 10.2139/ssrn.4135305) fitted orientation-dependent J-C parameters: flat build A=178.7 MPa, B=734.5 MPa, n=0.56, C=0.017; vertical A=182.8 MPa, B=2159.5 MPa, n=0.77, C=0.014; horizontal A=191.9 MPa, B=1044.9 MPa, n=0.65, C=0.004. The strain-rate coefficient C was small in all cases, confirming weak rate hardening in as-built LPBF AlSi10Mg (ghisi2022theinfluenceof pages 13-14, ghisi2022theinfluenceof pages 10-13).

**Zerilli-Armstrong model.** The Z-A model is physically based and distinguishes FCC from BCC crystal behavior. For FCC aluminum, it includes thermally activated dislocation glide terms. El-Aty et al. (2024; DOI: 10.3390/ma17071584) fitted a modified Z-A model to AA2060 at 100–500°C and 0.01–10 s⁻¹, obtaining C₁=498 MPa, C₂=125.34 MPa, n=0.51, C₃=0.0042, C₄=0.0066, C₅=0.0184, C₆=0.0001 (elaty2024modellingtheflow pages 6-9). Comparative studies suggest Z-A better captures the interaction between strain hardening and thermal softening at high cutting speeds above 200 m/min for Al 6061 (radhi2026thermomechanicalnumericalsimulation pages 3-4). This claim is moderately supported.

---

### 4. Applications Requiring Rate-Dependent Data

**Crashworthiness.** Vehicle crash events produce local strain rates of approximately 500 s⁻¹ in folding regions, with higher rates possible locally (smerd2005highstrainrate pages 1-3). Ubertalli et al. (2020) emphasized that reliable dynamic material data are essential for crashworthiness simulations of body-in-white aluminum components, as UTS increases 13–14% and elongation 75–105% at dynamic rates versus static (ubertalli2020highstrainrate pages 6-8). This is strongly supported.

**Bird strike.** EASA CS-25.631 requires aircraft to sustain impact with a 4 lb (1.8 kg) bird at cruise speed at sea level, or 0.85 cruise speed at 8000 ft (chen2023designforbird pages 1-4). For empennage structures, an 8 lb (3.6 kg) bird criterion applies (guida2008studydesignand pages 16-22). Strain rates during bird impact are characteristic of the 10²–10³ s⁻¹ range. McCarthy et al. (2004; DOI: 10.1023/b:acma.0000037133.64496.13) modeled 2024-T3 aluminum layers in fibre-metal-laminate leading edges but notably excluded strain-rate dependency for aluminum, assuming rate effects arose from the glass layers—a simplification that may not be conservative (mccarthy2004modellingofbird pages 7-10).

**Fan-blade-out containment and ballistic protection.** The FAA Uncontained Engine Debris Mitigation Program specifically investigates 2024-T351 aluminum because it is common in aircraft structures around engines. Engine-rotor failures produce high-velocity fragments, requiring constitutive models calibrated across relevant strain rates, temperatures, and stress states (seidt2010plasticdeformationand pages 18-22). This strongly supports the need for rate-dependent data.

**Forming.** Sheet-metal forming operations produce strain rates of approximately 10⁰–10² s⁻¹, while electromagnetic forming can reach ~3500 s⁻¹ (bhujangrao2020reviewofintermediate pages 1-3, smerd2005highstrainrate pages 1-3). Rate-dependent data are needed for constitutive models in stamping simulations and for predicting springback in rate-sensitive materials.

---

### 5. Other Test Settings That Change the Result

**Specimen size, geometry, and gauge length.** Yield strength and UTS are largely insensitive to specimen geometry (round vs. flat, standard vs. sub-size), but elongation is strongly affected. Masete et al. (2018; DOI: 10.1088/1757-899x/430/1/012015) found approximately 10% difference in elongation for different gauge lengths in Ti-6Al-4V, with UTS unaffected; specimens with matched L/√A ratios produced more comparable elongation results (only 6% difference) than specimens matched by L/W ratio (14% difference) (masete2018theeffectof pages 1-4, masete2018theeffectof pages 4-6). This principle applies to aluminum alloys as well.

ISO 6892-1 uses proportional specimens with k = L₀/√A₀ = 5.65 (the "A5.65" convention), while ASTM E8 uses k = 4.51 (moura2020ahighlyaccurate pages 1-3, doksanovic2018stress–strainrelationshipsand pages 4-7). The A50 (50 mm fixed gauge length) and A80 (80 mm) conventions in ISO 6892-1 are non-proportional and produce elongation values that cannot be directly compared with proportional specimens without correction. Dokšanović et al. (2018; DOI: 10.13167/2018.16.5) reported that increasing gauge length from 40 to 90 mm changed strain at fracture by up to 35.8%, while modulus of elasticity varied by ~9.6% and strain at yield by ~8.1% (doksanovic2018stress–strainrelationshipsand pages 9-12).

For aluminum specifically, Pourhassan et al. (2017; DOI: 10.1016/j.prostr.2017.07.198) found that standard versus non-standard specimen geometries for 2024-T3 ALCLAD produced yield strengths of 304 versus 290 MPa (4.6% difference), while ductility was nearly identical (pourhassan2017materialpropertiesof pages 4-6). Ubertalli et al. (2020) confirmed that short (10 mm) and long (80 mm) gauge-length specimens overlapped almost completely in stress-strain behavior for AA6016 (ubertalli2020highstrainrate pages 3-6). This is moderately supported.

**Surface condition: as-built versus machined LPBF.** Ghisi et al. (2022) emphasized that machined LPBF specimens remove surface defects and produce better apparent properties, so machined results may not represent net-shape AM parts (ghisi2022theinfluenceof pages 1-2). García-Zapata et al. (2024; DOI: 10.3390/ma17153655) reported that at 60 µm layer height, as-built surface roughness was Ra = 25 µm (Rz = 126 µm), and vertical specimens showed 19% lower resistance and 64% lower ductility than flat specimens; at 30 µm layer height, reductions were 7% and 47%, respectively (garciazapata2024effectsofbuilding pages 19-22). This strongly supports the need to report surface condition.

**Build orientation.** For LPBF AlSi10Mg, build orientation is the most influential parameter on both quasi-static and dynamic properties (amir2022studyonthe pages 10-11, amir2022studyonthe pages 1-2). Vertical specimens exhibit lower strain-to-failure because loading is parallel to columnar grains and perpendicular to melt-pool boundaries (ghisi2022theinfluenceof pages 4-6). Kan et al. (2019; DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2019.100805) found horizontal (X) specimens had YS of 307±11 MPa versus vertical (Z) YS of 210±8 MPa—a 32% reduction attributed to unfavorably oriented lack-of-fusion defects (kan2019factorsthataffect pages 19-23). This is strongly supported (202 citations).

**Test temperature and soak.** Temperature strongly interacts with strain rate. Vilamosa et al. (2015; DOI: 10.1051/epjconf/20159404018) showed that AA6060 has negligible SRS below 200°C but exhibits strong positive SRS at higher temperatures, with both yielding and work hardening affected (this finding from their abstract). The coupled strain-rate and temperature sensitivity is challenging to capture with most existing constitutive models.

**Strain measurement method.** Clip-on extensometers provide standard gauge-length-averaged strain but cannot capture post-necking local strain. Video extensometers and DIC provide full-field strain measurement. Hedayati et al. (2017; DOI: 10.1051/meca/2016060) showed that DIC strain measurement error can be less than 2% compared to clip-on extensometer when properly configured. DIC is essential for high-rate testing where contact extensometers cannot be used. Pourhassan et al. (2017) demonstrated good agreement between clip-on extensometer and DIC for standard aluminum tensile specimens (pourhassan2017materialpropertiesof pages 4-6).

**Machine stiffness.** Machine compliance affects the actual specimen strain rate during crosshead-controlled testing. Clinch (1997) analyzed that machine stiffness can produce yield-strength variations up to 2.69 ksi (~18.5 MPa) depending on machine hardness and elastic strain-rate range (clinch1997thevariationin pages 41-46). Open-loop machines produced higher yield strengths and greater scatter than closed-loop extensometer-controlled machines (clinch1997thevariationin pages 46-51).

---

### Recommendations for the BYU Vertical Cloud Lab

Based on this review, the following recommendations emerge for a lab designing LPBF aluminum alloys and testing room-temperature tensile bars:

1. **Report strain rate explicitly.** Always report the actual strain rate used, the control method (crosshead vs. extensometer feedback), and the standard followed (ASTM E8/B557 or ISO 6892-1 Method A/B). The ISO 6892-1 Method A strain-rate ranges (0.00025 s⁻¹ through yield, 0.0067 s⁻¹ post-yield) provide better reproducibility than crosshead control.

2. **Use consistent specimen geometry.** Report gauge length, cross-section dimensions, and the slimness ratio k. For LPBF, test in multiple build orientations (at minimum horizontal and vertical) and report surface condition (as-built or machined).

3. **For elevated-temperature and rate-dependent testing to add**, consider:
   - **Intermediate-rate servo-hydraulic testing** (1–100 s⁻¹) per ISO 26203-2 for crashworthiness data
   - **Split Hopkinson bar testing** (10²–10⁴ s⁻¹) if ballistic or impact applications are targeted
   - **Strain-rate jump tests** to efficiently measure m on single specimens
   - **Hot compression/tension** at temperatures and rates relevant to forming (300–500°C, 10⁻³–10⁻¹ s⁻¹) with Zener-Hollomon analysis

4. **Be aware of PLC effects** in Al-Mg-containing LPBF alloys: negative SRS and serrated flow can occur in specific strain-rate and temperature windows, complicating constitutive modeling and forming operations.

5. **When fitting J-C parameters**, always report the reference strain rate, the range of strain rates and temperatures used for calibration, and the build orientation for LPBF materials. Parameters are not universal constants—they are calibration-specific.

info.query: How do test settings, especially strain rate, change the measured tensile properties of aluminum alloys, and how should a lab choose and report them? Cover, with citations and DOIs: (1) Quasi-static rate: ASTM E8/E8M and B557 rate limits, ISO 6892-1 Method A (strain-rate control, ranges such as 0.00007, 0.00025, 0.0067 and 0.025 1/s) versus Method B, crosshead versus extensometer control, and how much yield strength, UTS and elongation shift across these ranges for 2xxx, 5xxx, 6xxx and 7xxx alloys and for LPBF AlSi10Mg. (2) Strain-rate sensitivity: the exponent m, negative strain-rate sensitivity and Portevin-Le Chatelier serrations in Al-Mg alloys and in LPBF aluminum, strain-rate jump and stress-relaxation tests that measure m on one specimen, and coupling of temperature and rate (Zener-Hollomon parameter, dynamic strain aging, superplastic forming windows). (3) Intermediate and high rates: servo-hydraulic high-speed tensile testing (1-1000 1/s, ISO 26203-2), drop-weight towers, split Hopkinson (Kolsky) tension and compression bars (10^2-10^4 1/s), Taylor impact and plate impact; specimen design, load ringing and adiabatic heating; and constitutive models (Johnson-Cook, Zerilli-Armstrong) fitted for 2024, 6061, 7075 and LPBF AlSi10Mg, with parameter values. (4) Applications that need rate data: crashworthiness, bird strike, fan-blade-out containment, ballistic and blast protection, and forming. (5) Other settings that change the result: specimen size and geometry (sub-size, round versus flat), gauge length and the elongation definition (A5 versus A50 mm), surface condition (as-built versus machined LPBF), build orientation, test temperature and soak, machine stiffness, and the strain-measurement method (clip-on extensometer, video extensometer, digital image correlation). Context: the BYU Vertical Cloud Lab designs aluminum alloys for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) with AI and CALPHAD, including critical-mineral-lean compositions (less Sc, Li, Ce), makes its own powder by ultrasonic atomization, and tests in a ladder of single tracks, density cubes and room-temperature tensile bars. It is deciding which elevated-temperature, non-tensile and rate-dependent mechanical tests to add. Prefer primary sources, NASA, NIST and AFRL technical reports, MMPDS and standards; give DOIs or report numbers; give numbers with temperatures, exposure times, strain rates and units; and say which claims are strongly vs. weakly supported.
